title: Bitwidth Fallback Policy and KV-aware Execution Path for Low-Bit Models (Draft)
content:
Purpose
This doc defines a pragmatic, deployable fallback and dispatch policy for low-bit quantized model variants (INT8 / FP8 / GPTQ / AWQ) in the serving runtime, with special attention to KV-cache compatibility and scheduling implications. The goal is to allow high-throughput, low-cost execution while preserving latency SLOs and avoiding correctness regressions caused by inappropriate fallbacks or cache mismatches.

Scope
- Kernel capability and constraint metadata required by the scheduler.
- Fallback triggers and priority order across quant variants and float16 baseline.
- KV cache compatibility rules and cache-key metadata additions.
- Interaction with batching and continuous token streaming.
- Rollout and testing plan for gradual enablement.

Non-goals
- New quantization algorithms or training-time transforms (this is runtime behavior only).
- Deep performance micro-optimizations for specific GPU kernels (left to kernel owners once policy is stable).

Background and motivation
We support multiple low-bit model variants in the model catalog to reduce cost. However, not every GPU/kernel supports every quant format equally. Also, KV cache layout and numerical drift differ between variants — blind fallback can produce cache mismatches (wrong outputs, subtle context corruption), and mixed-precision batching can increase jitter. This doc sets rules to avoid those failure modes while maximizing served throughput.

Key principles
1) Safety-first: never reuse a KV cache produced by a model variant that is not provably compatible (see compatibility section).
2) Predictability: honor per-request latency SLO and avoid sudden OOMs by conservative resource checks before dispatch.
3) Cost-awareness: prefer lower-bit compatible variants when safe; fall back to higher-precision (fp16) only when necessary.
4) Observability: every fallback decision must be logged with reason codes and metrics for postmortem and ML-eval alignment.

Kernel capability metadata
Each kernel build / device driver must expose a small metadata blob to the runtime during feature discovery. Required fields (runtime-internal keys):
- kernel_id (string)
- supported_bitwidths (list of strings): e.g., ["int8", "fp8", "gptq", "awq", "fp16"]
- max_seq_len (int)
- max_batch_tokens (int)
- kv_format_id (string): canonical id representing internal KV layout (e.g., "kv-v2-transposed-groupsize16")
- deterministic_prefix_attention (bool): whether attention math is deterministic under reordering
- numeric_error_profile (string): one of ["low","medium","high"] from empirical tests on key prompts
- memory_overhead_ratio (float-as-string): estimated extra device memory overhead for this kernel in percent (e.g., "0.12" for 12%)

Note: JSON schema above is runtime-only (these fields are flattened into scheduler tables). The runtime will refresh metadata on agent start and when new kernels are loaded.

Quant variant constraints and recommended ordering
We define a preference ordering per model and per device that is computed at model onboarding time using a small battery of microbenchmarks (latency, per-token error vs fp16 baseline, KV-compatibility tests). The ordering is a list from preferred->fallback. Example policy template: 
1) AWQ on A100 with kernel kv-v2-... (preferred when numeric_error_profile=="low")
2) GPTQ on same device if AWQ unavailable
3) INT8 (grouped) on V100-class devices
4) FP8 if it offers lower latency for long sequences
5) FP16 (baseline)

Fallback triggers (runtime)
A fallback may occur at request-time if any of these conditions are true:
- Kernel not available for requested quant variant on selected device.
- Device reports insufficient memory for micro-batch + KV cache (check memory_overhead_ratio).
- Observed numeric degradation: runtime-side eval probes (see below) exceed a per-customer threshold (configurable).
- Hardware error / kernel failure (OOM, illegal memory access, kernel crash).
- Forced operator incompatibility: e.g., attention op shape not supported by quant kernel.

When a fallback is triggered, we follow a conservative escalation: try next variant in the onboarded preference list that is both device-supported and KV-compatible; if none, fallback to fp16. All decisions produce metric events: fallback_reason, from_variant, to_variant, request_id, latency_impact_est.

KV cache compatibility rules
KV caches are sensitive: layout, dtype, and numerical differences can invalidate reuse. We define compatibility levels: 
- Exact (same kv_format_id and same quantization dtype): safe to reuse.
- Semantically compatible (different internal layout but known conversion path): reuse allowed if runtime performs an explicit conversion and conversion error < threshold. Conversion codecs must be explicit and registered (codec_id, cost_estimate).
- Incompatible: never reuse.

Cache key extensions
Cache keys MUST include: model_id, model_version, quant_variant_id, kv_format_id, sequence_prefix_hash, device_arch_tag. This guarantees we never accidentally reuse an incompatible cache between quant variants or across different kernel families. For semantically compatible conversions, the runtime will write a new cache entry with the target kv_format_id after conversion to prevent re-conversion on subsequent hits.

Cross-quant cache conversion
We allow explicit conversions for a small set of paths (e.g., gptq->int8, int8->fp16) when the conversion codec is available and conversion_cost_ms << token_latency_budget. Conversion must be synchronous and chargeable to the request. Conversion is only allowed when: 
- conversion_codec exists and is registered
- estimated conversion latency < 20% of request SLO left for the current token
- conversion numeric_error_profile == "low"

Scheduling and mixed-precision batching
The scheduler must avoid silently mixing KV caches from different quant families in the same micro-batch. Policies: 
- Micro-batches are homogenous by quant_variant_id and kv_format_id. If a request needs a direct fallback to a different variant, it must either be dispatched as its own micro-batch or converted prior to joining an existing batch.
- Continuous (token-at-a-time) streams: maintain per-stream state with pinned variant unless a safe online upgrade is possible (conversion path or identical kv_format_id).
- Batching heuristics: prefer grouping by (quant_variant_id, model_version, device_arch_tag) to maximize kernel throughput; only split when latency budgets demand it.

Memory accounting and admission control
Before admitting a request to a device, the resource manager will compute worst-case device memory = model_state + live_kv_bytes + (batch_tokens * per_token_scratch) * memory_overhead_ratio. If worst-case exceeds device available memory, the runtime will attempt: 
1) Try next preferred variant with smaller memory_overhead_ratio.
2) If none, reject with 429/QUEUE (per policy) rather than risking OOM.

Observability and metrics
Emit the following for every request (minimum):
- model_id, variant_requested, variant_served, fallback_reason ("none" if not used).
- kv_hit: boolean and kv_format_id.
- conversion_performed: codec_id or "none".
- per-token_latency_ms and p95_token_latency_ms.
- numeric_drift_score (where available) computed against short golden prompts run periodically.

Testing and verification harness
Model onboarding tests must include: 
- KV roundtrip correctness: generate sequences, save KV with variant A, reload with variant A and with candidate conversion paths; compute token-wise divergence.
- Stress tests: batch mixes across variants to validate micro-batch isolation.
- Memory safety: worst-case allocation simulated.
- Throughput/latency sweep: measure per-token latency at several batch sizes.

Rollback and rollout plan
1) Internal canary: enable policy on 5% of traffic for non-production models; watch metrics for fallback rate, numeric_drift_score, and errors.
2) Expand to 25% with alert thresholds locked in (fallback_rate > 2% triggers stop).
3) Customer can opt-out via tenant config until policy reaches GA.

Implementation notes and API surface
- New runtime flags: --enable-quant-fallback, --kv-conversion-ttl-ms (controls conversion timeout).
- New scheduler table: VariantPreference(model_id, device_arch_tag) as a flattened CSV-like string stored in metadata service.
- Kernel registration API must expose kv_format_id and memory_overhead_ratio at load time.

Open questions / tradeoffs
- Numeric error thresholds: how to set thresholds per customer (some customers tolerate more drift). Proposal: per-tenant guard rails with defaults derived from onboarding tests.
- Conversion cost accounting: should conversions be billed separately? Recommend yes for transparency.
- Fine-grained prefix trimming: can we safely reuse partial kv caches across variants when only later layers differ? Complex; defer to future work.

Next steps
- Implement kernel metadata additions in runtime agent (PR #1834).
- Add KV-conversion codec registry and two example codecs (gptq->int8, int8->fp16).
- Run onboarding harness for top-10 hosted models and publish preference lists to catalog.
- Draft tenant opt-out UI and API.

Appendix: example metric event
{\n  "request_id":"r_abc123",\n  "model_id":"gpt-medium-v2",\n  "variant_requested":"gptq-v2",\n  "variant_served":"int8-v1",\n  "fallback_reason":"OOM_ON_KERNEL",\n  "kv_hit":false,\n  "conversion_performed":"none",\n  "p95_token_latency_ms":55\n}

Notes to reviewers
Please focus review on the KV compatibility rules and whether the conversion constraints are practical for our common devices. Also flag any scheduler constraints that would cause unacceptable latency regressions for token streaming workloads.
